subtitle: Get to know the purpose of the DHS Equity Policy, then practice preparing an analysis and following through on a decision within your own role.
scope: For employees throughout DHS, using practice DSD communication examples. Consult the official policy and designated agency guidance for actual requirements and procedures.
introTranscript: The DHS Equity Policy connects equity to the work employees do every day. This course explains the difference between policy responsibility and learning practice, then follows a practice recurring notice through a decision, analysis preparation, evidence review, recommendation, and follow-through. You will practice useful questions and clear reasoning without treating a course note as an official analysis or approval. Work through the six lessons at your own pace, and return to the activities when they are useful. Completing this course does not replace required agency training or the applicable equity analysis process.

lessons.title: Read the policy as a guide to your work
lessons.summary: Distinguish an agency responsibility from the practice offered by this course.
lessons.objective: Identify the DHS Equity Policy’s connection to decisions and everyday work.

intro.heading: A policy is more than a statement of values
intro.body:
The DHS Equity Policy connects equity considerations to decisions and everyday work. Its purpose includes examining barriers and reducing inequitable effects on the people DHS serves and on employees. It applies to DHS employees across roles, rather than only to people whose job title includes equity. Read the official document when you need its requirements, and use the person or area responsible in the agency for current procedural guidance.

This course takes a practice work situation and helps you reason through it. A team is preparing a recurring service notice. You will consider what might affect recipients, which decision remains open, how to prepare an analysis, and how to review what happens afterward. These are instructional examples. They do not establish that a particular official notice has been analyzed, approved, or released.

Keep three things separate: the official policy, the applicable analysis or training requirement, and this course’s practice. The policy remains the source of duties. Your agency’s required process determines the appropriate tool and records. A learning reflection can help you prepare, but it cannot stand in for those steps. This distinction allows you to learn freely while taking your actual responsibilities seriously.

items.title: Official policy
items.body: The published DHS policy states responsibilities and procedures. A course summary is an aid to understanding, not a new policy or authority to change the requirements.

items.title: Applicable process
items.body: The DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit and guidance from the area responsible for equity help staff carry out required analysis. Check the current procedure for your work area rather than inventing a substitute.

items.title: Course practice
items.body: A practice scenario gives you room to test a question or compare options. It does not count as an analysis of an actual action or as completion of DHS-required training.

lessons.title: Find the decision inside the task
lessons.summary: Make an equity review specific enough to inform an action.
lessons.objective: State the open decision in a practice recurring-notice task.
objectives: State the open decision in a practice recurring-notice task.
Identify who may experience the effects of that decision.
Distinguish a change you can make from one that needs another role’s authority.
takeaways: Start with the decision, not a broad promise to improve equity.
Consider recipients, staff, and partners affected by the process.
Keep the responsible decision role clear.
lessons.statement: A specific decision gives your questions a purpose and your findings a place to go.

image.caption: A clear task helps staff connect analysis to something that can still change.

intro.heading: Move from a broad subject to a decision
intro.body:
In this example, a team says it will examine equity in service communication. That is a worthwhile subject, but it is too broad to guide the next notice. What is the actual decision? The team may be choosing the wording, delivery methods, response period, or contact route. Each choice has different effects and may belong to a different responsible role.

Describe the decision in a sentence. For example: “We need to decide how recipients will understand and respond to a recurring contact-preference notice.” Then identify the people and conditions involved. Recipients need usable information; staff need a manageable way to receive responses; partners may support communication. Ask whose experience could help you understand the process, and avoid assuming that one participant represents every recipient.

You can contribute even when you do not approve the final action. An analyst might identify an unclear instruction and offer wording options. A manager might control the response period. An accessibility contact might support a usable format. Naming these roles helps the team act on findings rather than pass around a general concern. It also helps you recognize when the actual decision belongs in the applicable analysis and review process.

accordion.heading: Clarify the work before analyzing it

items.title: Decision
items.body: Describe what is being chosen or changed. “Communication equity” is a subject; “how people will receive and respond to this notice” identifies a decision you can examine.

items.title: Effects
items.body: Consider the path from receipt through understanding and response. A change can make work easier for one participant while shifting effort or delay to another.

items.title: Role
items.body: Name who can revise, advise, or approve each part of the action. Do not confuse your ability to identify a concern with authority to decide every response.

tabs.label: Too broad
tabs.body: Make all service communication equitable. This expresses an intention but does not identify the current choice, the affected process, or the responsibility for changing it.

tabs.label: Specific
tabs.body: Choose a usable explanation and response process for the contact-preference notice before release. This identifies work that can be examined and changed.

tabs.label: Role-aware
tabs.body: Draft wording options, ask the access contact about format, and raise the response-period concern with the decision lead. This connects the specific issues to appropriate roles.

check.question: Which statement gives the review the clearest focus?
check.correct: Before release, compare how recipients can understand and respond to the recurring contact-preference notice.
wrong: Everyone should care more about equity.
The team should review everything it has ever done.
A staff member should decide recipients’ needs from their demographic identities.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement names a task, timing, and the experience to examine. It gives evidence and options a practical purpose.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A general appeal, an unlimited scope, or identity-based assumptions will not guide this decision. Start with the action that can still change.

sorting.heading: Decision, affected experience, or responsible role?

items.text: How long to allow for a response.
Whether the recipient can understand the requested action.
The manager responsible for the response process.
Which delivery options to use.

scenario.context: In this example, a team is considering a shorter response period. Staff can see possible access concerns, but the deadline is owned by another section. Someone suggests ignoring it because the team cannot change it directly.
options: Describe the concern and evidence, and bring it to the responsible section through the applicable review process.
Treat the deadline as fair because it belongs to another section.
Change it independently without checking the authority or procedure.
responses: The team can contribute useful analysis without claiming authority it does not have. Identify what information would help the responsible role decide.
Ownership elsewhere does not establish fairness or remove a relevant concern. You can raise the issue accurately.
A concern does not grant authority to change an official condition. Use the right process and responsible role.

lessons.transfer: Describe one open decision in your work in a single sentence. Who may be affected, and who can decide each part?

move.failure: Broad concerns can be discussed repeatedly without reaching a decision someone can change.

lessons.title: Use the required analysis process
lessons.summary: Keep the official analysis tool distinct from a short learning checklist.
lessons.objective: Identify the policy’s stated trigger for formal analysis in a practice long-term action.

intro.heading: Check the requirement before calling the work done
intro.body:
The published policy requires a formal equity analysis for actions with prolonged or long-term impact scheduled for leadership approval. It identifies the DHS Equity Analysis or Equity Scan within the toolkit, or a customized tool developed in consultation with an equity director for the business function. Use the official document and current agency guidance for the precise requirement and how it applies to your work.

In the practice notice example, the team is changing a recurring response procedure rather than simply correcting a typo. Staff should not decide that a four-question reflection fulfills the formal process. The reflection may identify useful concerns, but the team needs to clarify the applicable tool, who prepares the analysis, how affected perspectives are included, and where the analysis accompanies the proposed action.

Do not respond to uncertainty by inventing a waiver or an extra requirement. Bring the specific question to the responsible work-area equity contact or decision lead. Explain the action, its intended duration, the approval path, and the information already available. That makes the procedural conversation useful. The goal is a supported decision with the appropriate analysis, not merely a box marked complete.

lessons.keyStatement: Use the applicable analysis tool and process; do not rename a reflection as compliance.

items.title: Personal preparation
items.body: A note about who may be affected, barriers, and possible options can help you begin. Keep it labeled as preparation until the applicable analysis work is actually completed.

items.title: Applicable tool
items.body: Confirm which DHS analysis or scan applies, or whether a customized option was developed through the policy’s stated consultation route. Convenience alone does not establish approval.

items.title: Decision packet
items.body: Clarify how the analysis is provided with the action for review. A completed learning activity does not establish that the analysis reached the responsible decision role.

tabs.label: Reflection note
tabs.body: Three observations and two questions about the notice. Useful for preparation, but not evidence that the required analysis was completed through the applicable procedure.

tabs.label: Draft analysis
tabs.body: An analysis is being prepared with identified evidence gaps. Calling it a draft preserves the distinction between work underway and the supported product needed for review.

tabs.label: Completed applicable process
tabs.body: The team can identify the tool used, the actual action examined, and the analysis provided for decision review. This claim needs the real work and records behind it.

check.question: The team completed a short course checklist for a proposed long-term procedure change. What should it do before calling the formal analysis complete?
check.correct: Confirm and carry out the applicable DHS analysis process; keep the course checklist as preparation rather than a substitute.
wrong: Rename the checklist “approved analysis” because it asks equity questions.
Assume formal analysis is unnecessary whenever the change is intended to help.
State that this course gave permission to skip the toolkit.
check.feedbackCorrect: You preserve the checklist’s useful preparation while recognizing that the required process has its own tool, action, and records.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A title, helpful intention, or course activity does not waive the official procedure. Clarify and complete the applicable process.

items.text: List questions about the proposed recurring procedure.
Complete the appropriate DHS analysis or scan for the actual action.

lessons.title: Bring evidence and perspectives together
lessons.summary: Use accounts and records to compare effects without overstating what either proves.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a record, a participant account, and an untested explanation.
objectives: Distinguish a record, a participant account, and an untested explanation.
Identify a missing perspective relevant to the notice decision.
Explain an evidence gap without dismissing the information already available.
takeaways: Records and people’s accounts answer different questions.
A difference in results needs investigation, not an identity-based explanation.
lessons.statement: A useful analysis shows what supports a conclusion and what you still need to learn.

image.caption: People’s accounts can help explain a pattern while leaving room for other experiences.

intro.heading: Do not make one source answer every question
intro.body:
The practice team has response counts and several accounts from recipients. Counts can show how many replies arrived within a period, provided the records and denominator are reliable. Accounts can describe where an instruction was confusing or a response route was difficult. Neither source answers every question. A count does not reveal motive, and a small set of accounts does not represent everyone.

Compare the information against the decision. If the team is choosing response options, it needs to know which conditions matter to using those options. Invite relevant perspectives and ask about the task rather than about presumed group traits. If one perspective is missing, state the gap and consider a useful way to hear it before the decision. Do not invent the missing account or assign someone the job of representing an entire community.

An evidence gap does not make the existing information worthless. It changes the confidence and scope of the conclusion. You might recommend testing a clearer opening because several recipients identified the same confusing sentence, while also saying the team has not yet examined other delivery methods. Keep evidence, interpretation, and proposed action separate enough that someone else can review your reasoning.

lessons.keyStatement: Use the information for the question it can answer, and state the limits.

accordion.heading: Three parts of a supported conclusion

items.title: Information
items.body: Describe the source, context, and question it addresses. A reply count and a voluntary comment are both information, but they should not be interpreted as if they were the same measure.

items.title: Interpretation
items.body: Explain what you think the information suggests. Keep other plausible explanations visible. A pattern by area does not identify a person’s preference or establish its cause.

items.title: Gap
items.body: Name the missing information and why it matters to the decision. Decide whether it needs to be obtained before the choice or reviewed after a proportionate, authorized test.

tabs.label: Count
tabs.body: The team received twenty replies from forty notices by Friday. Check the contact list, period, and duplicate handling before comparing the figure with another release.

tabs.label: Account
tabs.body: A willing recipient says the opening did not explain the requested action. This is a specific concern the team can investigate, not a population estimate.

tabs.label: Combined reasoning
tabs.body: The team tests a clearer opening and checks both comprehension feedback and response patterns. The combined information can strengthen the review while leaving causation limits visible.

check.question: Which conclusion uses a participant account appropriately?
check.correct: The account identifies a specific confusing instruction to investigate; the team should not generalize it to every recipient.
wrong: One account proves the entire population has the same difficulty.
An account is useless unless it represents everyone.
The person’s identity alone explains why they had difficulty.
check.feedbackCorrect: You preserve the account’s practical value and its limits. A specific concern can inform a test without becoming a universal claim.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The alternatives overgeneralize, dismiss useful information, or replace investigation with an identity-based explanation.

items.text: Three readers identified the same confusing sentence.
A clearer opening may help recipients identify the action.
The revised wording has not yet been tested.
The reply count increased after several process changes.
The wording may have contributed to the increase.
The effect of the delivery change is not isolated.

scenario.context: In this example, a team has response records and feedback from willing users of one response method. It has not heard from people who use another method. A staff member wants to say the review represents all recipients.
options: State who contributed, identify the missing perspective, and arrange a useful way to examine it before drawing a broad conclusion.
Assume the missing group has the same experience because the task is similar.
Remove all feedback because the review is incomplete.
responses: This keeps the useful information and makes the limit visible. The next step should fit how important the gap is to the decision.
A similar task does not establish the same conditions or experience. Check the relevant perspective rather than supplying it.
The available accounts remain useful within their context. Incomplete evidence calls for bounded conclusions, not erasing what is known.

lessons.transfer: For one draft finding, write its source, what it supports, and what it does not establish.

move.control: You can distinguish evidence from interpretation and make a missing perspective visible.
move.failure: A convenient source can be made to stand for people or conditions it did not cover.
move.next: Add a specific evidence gap and a proportionate way to address it to the analysis draft.

lessons.title: Recommend a change with clear responsibility
lessons.summary: Connect a finding to an option, its tradeoffs, and the role that can act.
lessons.objective: Compare two notice options against the identified barrier and task.
objectives: Compare two notice options against the identified barrier and task.
Describe a recommendation with its evidence and uncertainty.
Identify the role responsible for the next action without transferring staff work to the consultant.
takeaways: A recommendation should connect a specific finding to a specific option.
Name tradeoffs and limits rather than promising a perfect solution.
Staff prepare their work; consultant guidance can strengthen it without replacing their responsibility.
lessons.statement: Support helps you improve your analysis; it does not make someone else responsible for doing all of it.

image.caption: A supported recommendation gives colleagues something concrete to consider.

intro.heading: Make the reasoning reviewable
intro.body:
The practice team is ready to recommend a clearer opening and usable response choices. The recommendation should explain what problem the change addresses, which evidence supports it, and what remains uncertain. It should also identify effort, timing, and responsibility. Without those details, a positive intention may never become a practical change.

Compare the recommendation with a realistic alternative. Keeping the original notice and adding a contact number may require less editing but leave the confusing action statement in place. Revising the explanation and response choices addresses more identified concerns but needs coordination and a check of whether the changes work. The comparison does not have to make one option look foolish. It should help the decision role understand the differences.

The consultant can offer guidance, knowledge, leadership, and feedback. Staff still develop their own analysis and carry the assigned work. Prepare a specific question when you seek support: explain the decision, evidence, options, and uncertainty. Formal authority remains with the responsible role. A consultant’s feedback, a course exercise, and a decision approval are different events; record and describe them accurately.

Describe a recommendation with its evidence and uncertainty.

lessons.keyStatement: A recommendation needs a reason, a next action, and someone who can carry it forward.

accordion.heading: What a reader needs to understand

items.title: Reason
items.body: Connect the option to the observed problem. Do not rely only on a general equity value statement. Show why the change may help people accomplish the task.

items.title: Tradeoff
items.body: Explain the effort, timing, or remaining limitation. A tradeoff is information to examine, not automatic proof that the option should be rejected.

items.title: Next responsibility
items.body: Name who prepares, decides, implements, and reviews the relevant part. Consultant support may improve the reasoning without taking over those roles.

tabs.label: Unclear
tabs.body: Improve equity in the notice. This does not tell the decision role what to change, why it matters, or how the team will carry it forward.

tabs.label: Overconfident
tabs.body: Adopt the new version because it will remove all barriers. This promises more than the evidence establishes and leaves no room for unresolved concerns.

tabs.label: Supported
tabs.body: Revise the identified confusing sentence and response route, confirm the usable format, test the changes, and review the remaining deadline concern with the responsible role.

check.question: Which request makes consultant feedback most useful?
check.correct: Here is the decision, evidence, options, and uncertainty; can you help me examine the missing perspective before I revise my analysis?
wrong: Please do the entire analysis for me so I do not need to understand it.
Approve this official action because I finished the course.
Tell me the conclusion without looking at the evidence or options.
check.feedbackCorrect: You keep responsibility for your work while asking a focused question that the consultant can help you examine.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Support should build your capability and strengthen your work. It does not replace preparation, grant unrelated formal authority, or eliminate the need for evidence.

items.text: Several participants found the opening unclear.
Revise the action statement and test it.
The editor prepares the revised draft.
The effect of the deadline remains uncertain.
Raise the deadline concern with supporting information.
The decision lead considers the proposed response period.

lessons.next: Next, review the change and communicate what the evidence supports.

scenario.context: A practice analyst sends the consultant a draft with two options. The consultant asks for a clearer explanation of a missing perspective. The analyst assumes this means the consultant will now write the whole report.
options: The analyst develops the missing section, using the feedback and a focused follow-up question when helpful.
The analyst stops work until the consultant supplies a finished report.
The analyst treats the feedback as formal approval of the proposed action.
responses: This uses support to strengthen staff capability and keeps the analysis moving. Clarify responsibilities if another role needs to supply evidence.
Feedback does not automatically transfer the assignment. Agree any actual change in responsibility rather than assuming one.
Feedback on reasoning is different from approval by the responsible decision role. Keep the distinction visible.

lessons.transfer: Draft a short recommendation for a task you help shape. Add the supporting finding, one limit, and the responsible next action.

move.control: You can prepare a supported draft and ask a focused question when you need guidance.
move.failure: A request for support can become an assumed transfer of responsibility.
move.next: Revise your own comparison using feedback, and confirm the next decision or implementation role.

lessons.title: Review the effect and keep the record accurate
lessons.summary: Describe what happened without equating a completed activity with equitable results.
lessons.objective: Separate a completed notice change from evidence about its effect.
objectives: Separate a completed notice change from evidence about its effect.
Choose a useful follow-up question and review responsibility.
Write a result statement that includes its evidence, limitation, and next step.
takeaways: An analysis and a released notice are activities, not proof of lasting improvement.
Review the effect relevant to the change and keep unresolved concerns visible.
Describe results in a way another person can examine.
lessons.statement: Follow-through connects the decision to what people experience afterward.

image.caption: A review can help the team retain a useful change and identify what still needs attention.

intro.heading: Finish the activity, then examine its effect
intro.body:
The practice team completed its applicable analysis, revised the notice, and released the new version through the responsible process. These are real activities in the example. To learn whether the change helped, the team needs a follow-up question that matches the problem it tried to address. Can recipients identify the requested action? Can they use the response choices? What concern remains?

Reviewing effects requires care with comparisons. A reply count may change because of wording, timing, delivery, or the contact list. A small voluntary review may reveal a remaining confusing step without establishing how common it is. State these conditions rather than attributing every improvement to the team’s preferred explanation. A useful review can support a next adjustment even when it does not establish a single cause.

Keep records appropriate to the actual work and its rules. Do not add names, diagnoses, or sensitive case details to course notes simply to make the exercise seem complete. In the real process, use the designated records and access practices. Identify who will review the result and when, then describe the completed action, the observed information, the limit, and the next step. That gives colleagues a clear basis for continued learning and accountability.

lessons.keyStatement: Report the activity and the evidence separately, then name the next useful adjustment.

accordion.heading: A result someone else can understand

items.title: Action
items.body: Describe the analysis and change actually completed. Do not imply that a proposal was implemented merely because it was written or reviewed.

items.title: Effect
items.body: Explain the information examined after the change and its context. A small test, a count, and a voluntary account each support different kinds of conclusions.

items.title: Next step
items.body: Name what should be retained, revised, investigated, or referred. Assign an appropriate role and review point without inventing a confirmed schedule for the broader program.

tabs.label: Activity record
tabs.body: The team completed the applicable analysis and revised the notice. This is a record of work done and does not alone establish a better experience for recipients.

tabs.label: Limited effect
tabs.body: Willing readers more readily identified the requested action in the revision. State the review context and avoid treating it as proof of universal access.

tabs.label: Continued work
tabs.body: Keep the clearer wording, check the response route after the next use, and raise the remaining deadline concern. This connects the finding to a practical follow-up.

check.question: Which report is appropriately bounded?
check.correct: The notice was revised; a small review suggests clearer instructions, while questions about the response period remain.
wrong: The team completed analysis, so every recipient now has equitable access.
The reply count rose, so the wording alone caused the increase.
A remaining question proves that all analysis and revision were useless.
check.feedbackCorrect: The report keeps the completed activity, limited evidence, and unresolved concern visible. That supports a useful next decision.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The alternatives confuse activity with effect, assume an isolated cause, or erase useful progress. State what happened and what the evidence can support.

sorting.heading: Action, effect evidence, or continued work?

items.text: The revised notice was released through the responsible process.
Several willing readers identified the action more easily.
Review whether the response route remains useful.
The team completed the applicable analysis.
Some recipients still described difficulty with the response period.
Raise the remaining deadline concern with the decision lead.

scenario.context: In this example, a team completed a procedure review and changed several parts of its notice process. The next reply count is higher. The manager asks for a public statement that the team eliminated inequity.
options: Describe the changes and observed improvement, state the comparison limits, and identify remaining access questions for review.
Make the broad claim because the team intended to advance equity.
Avoid mentioning any result because certainty is incomplete.
responses: This reports useful work and findings without claiming more than the evidence supports. The remaining questions can guide continued action.
Intention and effort do not establish that inequity was eliminated. A broad claim needs evidence the example does not supply.
You can communicate a bounded finding. Uncertainty should be visible, not used to hide the completed work or useful information.

lessons.transfer: For one actual change within your work, identify the completed activity, what effect you need to review, and the role responsible for the next step.

move.control: You can report the result accurately and maintain a clear next responsibility.
move.failure: A completed analysis can be mistaken for proof of the outcome it intended to support.
move.next: Write a short follow-up note with the action, evidence, limitation, and next review question.

jobAid.subtitle: Prepare clearly, use the applicable process, and follow through
remember: Locate the official policy and current work-area guidance.
Name the actual decision and responsible roles.
Confirm the applicable analysis tool and review path.
Keep evidence, interpretation, and missing perspectives distinct.
Prepare a recommendation with its tradeoffs and uncertainty.
Review effects without overstating the result.

sections.heading: Before an action is reviewed
items: What is changing, for how long, and through which approval route?
Which applicable analysis or scan should accompany the action?
Whose perspective and what evidence are needed for the decision?

sections.heading: When seeking support
items: Explain the decision, evidence, options, and uncertainty.
Ask a focused question and keep responsibility for your own work.
Distinguish consultant feedback from formal decision authority.

sections.heading: After a change
items: Review the effect relevant to the barrier.
State the evidence limits and the next responsible step.
